common_name: Rio Verde Cabbage (Heat-Tolerant Blue-Green Fall Cabbage)

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens, sow in June-July for late-summer transplanting and a December-January harvest. Rio Verde is one of the longest-standing Texas A&M AgriLife-recommended cabbages precisely because it holds up through the lingering heat of a Gulf Coast September and October before sizing up in cooler weather.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants 15-18 inches apart in rows 24-36 inches apart, and keep moisture even as heads begin to fill out. Rio Verde is a main-season hybrid cabbage bred for exceptional tolerance of heat and humidity, producing large, slightly flattened, dense blue-green heads that commonly reach 4-6 pounds without splitting even when harvest is delayed. It has been a long-running recommendation from Texas A&M AgriLife Extension and LSU AgCenter for southern fall gardens because it germinates and establishes reliably in late-summer heat that stalls many other cabbages, then finishes with good size and quality through the cooler months. Choose Rio Verde where a proven, widely adapted variety with a long track record in hot, humid climates matters more than novelty.

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before transplanting; sow in early summer for transplanting in July-August so heads mature during the cooler, drier stretch of a zone 8-9 fall and winter.

directions: Transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun, using tighter 12-inch spacing for smaller fresh-market heads or 18-24 inches for larger heads and kraut production. Bravo is a Bejo-bred hybrid valued for uniform, solid, blue-green round heads with good resistance to head cracking and to black rot and fusarium yellows, two disease pressures that build up quickly in warm, humid fall gardens. It has a reputation among market growers for performing well across a wide range of climates, from Deep South winter production to northern summer crops, which makes it a dependable second cabbage choice alongside more region-specific varieties. Feed consistently through head formation, since Bravo's large frame needs steady fertility to fill out its heads before a hard freeze.

common_name: Southern Comet Broccoli (Heat-Tolerant Hybrid AAS Broccoli)

planting.note: Start indoors 5-6 weeks before transplanting; in zone 8-9 gardens transplant in late August-September for a crop that heads through the milder, more forgiving fall temperatures instead of spring's fast run-up to heat.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants 18-24 inches apart with 3 feet between rows to give the large frame room to develop. Southern Comet is an All-America Selections-winning F1 hybrid selected specifically for its ability to hold up to heat and humidity better than most broccoli, forming dense, deep-green 8-inch domed heads that resist the loose, ricey curd broccoli often develops when temperatures spike during head formation. Its strong side-shoot production after the main head is cut extends the harvest window considerably, an advantage in southern fall gardens where the cool season is often shorter than the plant's full production potential. Keep soil evenly moist and side-dress with nitrogen after the first head is harvested to sustain shoot production into winter.

planting.note: Start indoors 5-6 weeks before transplanting; for zone 8-9 fall crops, transplant in late August-September so the long harvest window carries production through the cooler months without bolting.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants 14-20 inches apart in rows 24-36 inches apart. Umpqua is an open-pollinated variety developed at Territorial Seed Company in Oregon and named for the Umpqua River; it is prized for producing large, uniform, dark-green 5-8 inch heads with big beads that size up quickly, then continuing to yield heavily from side shoots over an unusually long harvest window. Because it is open-pollinated rather than a hybrid, home gardeners can save true-to-type seed from year to year, making it a good choice for growers who want to build a self-sufficient seed-saving rotation into their fall brassica planting. Its long production season rewards steady feeding and consistent moisture, since plants left to dry out or run short on nitrogen will cut the side-shoot harvest short.

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before transplanting; in zone 8-9 gardens transplant in August-September, adding roughly two extra weeks beyond the stated maturity to account for slower fall growth as light and temperatures decline.

directions: Transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants 18-24 inches apart with 24-36 inches between rows, and feed generously since Amazing needs vigorous leaf growth to protect its curd. This variety is valued for its self-blanching habit: large, upright wrapper leaves naturally curl in over the developing curd, shielding it from sun and weather so it stays creamy white without the hand-tying required by older cauliflower varieties. Amazing's extended, somewhat uneven maturity window is actually an asset for home gardeners, since plants in the same bed don't all come ready at once, spreading a single planting's harvest out over several weeks instead of demanding it all be used or preserved immediately. It is widely regarded as one of the more forgiving fall cauliflowers for gardeners still learning to time brassica plantings against the first frost.

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before transplanting; in zone 8-9 gardens transplant in July-August so curds finish sizing and coloring during the shorter, cooler days of fall, which deepens the purple pigment.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants 18-24 inches apart, and keep soil evenly moist since curds can lose color and flavor if plants are stressed by drought as they mature. Violet Queen is an open-pollinated cauliflower whose deep purple curds come from anthocyanin pigments, the same antioxidant compounds found in red cabbage and purple carrots, and the color contrasts strikingly with its dark green wrapper leaves in the garden. Because it is not a hybrid, seed can be saved from year to year, and the curds hold their purple color raw but fade to green when cooked, so it is best featured in salads, slaws, or briefly steamed dishes where the color matters. Harvest promptly once curds are full-sized, since heads left too long in warm or bright conditions can dull from vivid violet toward a duller, greener tone.
